subject: biology
title: Diffusion, active transport and bulk transport
key_idea: Substances cross membranes by passive methods that need no energy, and by active methods that use ATP. Diffusion moves particles down a gradient. Active transport moves them against it. Bulk transport moves large amounts in vesicles.

blocks.text: Passive transport needs no ATP. Particles move down a concentration gradient because of their own kinetic energy.

items.meaning: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient.
Diffusion directly through the phospholipid bilayer.
Diffusion through channel proteins or carrier proteins.

items: Small, non-polar molecules pass through the bilayer, such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and lipid-soluble substances.
The hydrophobic core limits movement. Ions and polar molecules, such as glucose, cannot cross easily.
Water is small enough to cross slowly between the phospholipids.
Channel proteins form a water-filled pore. Each is specific to certain ions or polar molecules, and some can open and close.
Carrier proteins bind a specific molecule, change shape and release it on the other side.
Both move substances down their gradient, so no ATP is used.
Rate levels off when all the proteins are in use. This is called saturation.
Passive transport is down a gradient and uses no ATP.
Simple diffusion crosses the bilayer, and only small non-polar molecules can do this easily.
Facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins for ions and polar molecules.

sections.heading: What affects the rate of transport

blocks.text: Several factors change how fast substances cross a membrane.

rows: Faster diffusion. A bigger difference gives a greater net movement.
Faster. More membrane means more room for particles to cross.
Faster, because the diffusion distance is shorter.
Faster facilitated diffusion, up to the point where all are in use.
Faster, because particles have more kinetic energy.

blocks.text: Cells are adapted for rapid transport by having more membrane or more proteins in it. The microvilli of epithelial cells in the ileum increase surface area. Cells with a lot of transport have many carrier proteins.

items: Rate rises with gradient, surface area and temperature, and with a shorter distance.
Facilitated diffusion also depends on how many proteins are present.
Adaptations increase membrane area or protein number.

blocks.text: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient. It needs energy from ATP.

items: A carrier protein binds the substance on one side of the membrane.
ATP is hydrolysed to ADP and phosphate, and the energy released changes the shape of the carrier.
The substance is released on the other side, at a higher concentration.
Only specific substances bind, because each carrier has a binding site of one shape.
Rate depends on how many carriers there are and how much ATP is available. Respiration inhibitors stop it.

blocks.text: Co-transport moves two substances at once using one carrier protein. The absorption of glucose in the ileum is the standard example.

items.text: Active transport removes sodium ions from the epithelial cell into the blood. This keeps sodium concentration inside the cell low.
Sodium ions diffuse from the gut lumen into the cell down a gradient, through a co-transporter protein.
The same protein carries glucose in, against its gradient. The glucose is carried along with the sodium ions.
Glucose then diffuses into the blood through a different protein, by facilitated diffusion.

items: Active transport goes against the gradient and uses ATP.
Carriers change shape using energy from ATP hydrolysis.
In co-transport, sodium moving down its gradient brings glucose in.

blocks.text: Large molecules and whole cells move in or out of cells in vesicles. This also needs ATP.

items.meaning: Bulk transport into a cell. The membrane folds in around the material and pinches off as a vesicle.
Bulk transport out of a cell. A vesicle fuses with the cell-surface membrane and releases its contents.

items: Endocytosis takes in large particles, such as a phagocyte engulfing a bacterium.
Exocytosis releases products such as enzymes and hormones, which have been packaged in vesicles by the Golgi apparatus.
Both processes use ATP, to move the vesicle and to change the shape of the membrane.
The membrane gained by endocytosis is balanced by the membrane lost in exocytosis.

items.text: Facilitated diffusion through a channel protein
Facilitated diffusion through a carrier protein
Active transport by a carrier protein

items: Endocytosis takes material in by a vesicle. Exocytosis sends it out.
Both need ATP.
Diffusion and facilitated diffusion are passive. Active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis are active.

blocks.text: Model cells show how size and conditions change the rate of diffusion.

items: Use agar blocks or Visking tubing containing a coloured substance or indicator.
Change one variable, such as the block size, temperature or concentration gradient.
Time how long the substance takes to diffuse in or out. Colour change or mass change can be used.
Control the other variables, and repeat to get a mean.
Change one variable and control the rest.
Time to diffuse measures the rate.

checks.q: Explain why glucose cannot cross a cell membrane by simple diffusion.
checks.a: Glucose is a large, polar molecule. It cannot pass through the hydrophobic core of the phospholipid bilayer, so it needs a protein to cross.

checks.q: Describe how active transport differs from facilitated diffusion.
checks.a: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient and uses energy from ATP hydrolysis. Facilitated diffusion moves substances down their gradient and uses no ATP.

checks.q: Explain how glucose is absorbed from the ileum into an epithelial cell by co-transport.
checks.a: Sodium ions are actively transported out of the cell, so the concentration of sodium is lower inside. Sodium ions diffuse in through a co-transporter protein. Glucose enters with them against its concentration gradient.
